newsitem.title: GERMANY: POLL - Mark shows no sign of revival vs dollar in '97.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Mark shows no sign of revival vs dollar in '97.

text.p: The mark shows no sign of recovering against the mighty dollar until early 1998, when the future of the single European currency becomes clear as initial members are selected, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

As has often been the case, the survey showed a wide disparity of opinion on the course of the dollar and reflected a range of about 30 pfennigs between the highest and lowest quarterly forecasts until the euro starts in January 1999.

The selection of inaugural members for the new euro is due to take place in the spring of 1998, a period when the dollar is expected to begin sliding toward 1.75 marks, according to the survey of 26 European financial institutions.
The dollar was expected to peak at 1.80 marks in the 1997 fourth quarter, a time when the 1997 finances of European Union nations will be scrutinised as to who can join EMU.
Volatile foreign exchange markets have thrown previous forecasts into disarray.
The last Reuters survey in April expected the mark to recover against the dollar in mid-1997, end the second quarter at 1.73 marks and modestly strengthen ahead of January 1999.
But in late European dealings on Tuesday, the dollar was trading above 1.81 marks, levels not seen since 1991.

Worries about starting European monetary union with a large number of member nations was seen as a chief cause of pressure on the mark, which showed a median level of 1.75 to the dollar in the 1998 fourth quarter in the survey.
"It is clearly based on insecurity about the start of currency union," said Eckhard Schulte, economist at IBJ Deutschland in Frnakfurt. "This is an untested project."
IBJ forecast that the dollar would end the 1997 third quarter at 1.85 marks and rise to 1.90 in the fourth quarter before peaking at 2.00 marks in the second and third quarters of 1998.
Schulte noted that the Maastricht Treaty says the European Central Bank will be independent from political forces, possibly even more so than the Bundesbank.
But he added: "Even if that is the case, we still do not know what kind of policies will be be implemented. Our outlook is for the mark to lose more ground."
But others said prospects for the German economic recovery to take hold and a modest downturn in the U.S. economy during 1998 would help the mark to recover.
"We look for a slowdown in the U.S. economy in the second half of 1998," said Nikolaus Keis, economist at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich. "This is not going to be a recession but a slowdown."

In addition, they said the risk premium built into the market because of uncertainty about the European currency -- namely that EMU will start with a large number of countries as entry will be based on political considerations -- will start to fade.

The mark also appeared set to catch its breath against the pound. The survey showed a median forecast of 3.00 marks in the 1997 third quarter and called for sterling to weaken steadily against the mark to 2.80 marks in the 1998 fourth quarter.

The yen should briefly gain ground against the mark in the run-up to the start of the new currency. The survey showed a median forecast of 63.90 yen to the mark in the third quarter before the yen rises to 61.50 per mark in the 1998 second quarter, but resumes its downtrend to 63.10 in the 1998 fourth quarter.
